_: The model ladder, as data. Nothing here is compiled into code.
`accepts` is what the agent may call itself in its own opening event, and
that event is the only trustworthy answer to what actually ran: asking for a
model is not the same as getting one, and effort suffixes have been dropped
It is a list because the runtime is not consistent. Rank 4 has been seen
answering `Cursor Grok 4.6 High` and, minutes later on the same launcher in
the same round, `Cursor Grok 4.6`. Both are that model; both are accepted.
A run that did the work is not thrown away over which spelling came back.
What does not widen is how the comparison is made. The short name is a
prefix of every other Grok 4.6 row here, and across the 214 models this
account can see there are 197 such prefix pairs — so a name is compared by
exact equality against the list, never by prefix and never by substring.
The first entry is the canonical one, printed by `resolve` and shown in
tables. Regenerate with `node scripts/models.mjs sync`, which reads
`agent --list-models`, adds any spelling it finds that is missing, drops
nothing, and refuses if an id has stopped existing.
_roles: A role is a default tier for work that `assess` never sees. It is a
starting point, not a judgement: a step the orchestrator has assessed
carries its own tier and never reads these.
`chip` sits at `medium` because medium is where ordinary work belongs —
a step against a clear plan, in a couple of files. It used to sit at
`high`, which made the strongest-but-one model the thing every unassessed
step got by default, and reaching was the norm rather than the exception.
Above medium is a claim about the step: `high` for work that is genuinely
hard, `xhigh` for the top of the ladder only. Below it is fine too —
`low` covers verification and light tasks perfectly well.
`refine` stays at `high` because it is one of the hard ones. It reads a
plan and decides the shape of the whole round — how many steps, what each
one owns, what waits on what — and a wrong answer there is not one step
re-run, it is the round built on the wrong skeleton.
_runners: A second way to execute a step. The ladder above is Cursor's and is left
exactly as it was: the two are separate things that happen to share a tier
vocabulary, and a row here is never compared against a row there.
opencode runs one model — DeepSeek V4 Flash — so a tier does not choose a
model, it chooses how hard the model thinks. `efforts` maps the five tiers
onto the three the model accepts (low, high, max), which means composer,
low and medium are all one effort. That collapse is real and is printed
rather than implied.
Where the collapse falls is a choice, and it follows the ladder's centre
of gravity. `medium` is the default tier, so it maps to `low` — the
model's ordinary effort — and not to `high`. Mapping it to `high` meant
every default step on this runner reached, which is the thing `high` is
supposed to be the exception for. `high` reaches; `xhigh` is the top.
`verifiable: false` is the important field. Cursor's log names the model
that answered, so a silent downgrade is caught; opencode's names nothing,
so it cannot be. With one model there is nothing to confuse it with, and
the record says what was asked for and marks itself unverified rather than
claiming a check it did not make.
What CAN be checked is that the effort is one this model accepts. opencode
keeps its own registry at `registry` below, and an effort outside that
model's `reasoning_options` is accepted in silence by `opencode run` — so
the launcher looks it up before spending anything.
_claude: Claude Code is the third runner, and the only one whose tier picks a MODEL
and an effort together — so it gets a `ladder` of its own rather than one
model and an `efforts` map. Sonnet carries the two light tiers; Opus takes
the default tier and everything above it, because the model is what buys
the quality here and the effort dial is what costs the wall clock.
`effort` is Claude Code's own `--effort` flag. `takesEfforts` below is its
full vocabulary — low, medium, high, xhigh, max — of which this ladder uses
only the bottom two, on purpose. The list is the binary's, not our usage,
so it stays whole. It is a separate key from the tier-to-effort `efforts`
map a single-model runner carries, because it is a different thing, and a row
naming an effort outside it is refused before the run rather than after
— the same guard opencode gets from its registry, except this list comes
from the binary's own --help rather than from a cache that may not exist.
Five tiers, three rungs. That is deliberate and it is what the ladder is
for on this runner: the effort dial is held DOWN on purpose. Against a
well-defined plan a higher effort mostly buys wall-clock — every step in a
wide round paying for reasoning the plan already did — so the ladder spends
on the model instead and stops climbing early.
So `high` and `xhigh` are one rung, and nothing sits above Opus at medium.
Marking a step `xhigh` is not wrong, it just does not buy anything here;
`assess` says so rather than letting the row imply a reach that is not
there. composer and low are one rung for the same reason lower down.
The consequence worth knowing: `medium` is the default tier, so ordinary
work runs on OPUS on this runner, not on Sonnet. Sonnet is what you get by
assessing a step down to `low` or `composer`, which is now a real choice
about cost rather than a formality.
`verifiable: true` because Claude Code names the model in its `system/init`
event, exactly where Cursor does — so `harvest.mjs` reads it with no new
code and a silent downgrade is caught. `accepts` is generous for the same
reason it is generous on the Cursor ladder: a run that did the work is not
thrown away over which spelling came back. If a dated snapshot id arrives,
`verify` says so by name and adding it here is the fix.
